concept.name: Yield curve
concept.definition: A curve that plots the yields of bonds of the same credit quality (typically government securities) against their times to maturity at a given point in time. The U.S. Treasury's official version is a par yield curve relating the par yield on a Treasury security to its time to maturity, derived daily from market price quotations.
concept.intuition: It is a snapshot of what it costs to borrow money for different lengths of time, showing how the market prices time, risk, and expectations about future rates.
concept.mechanics: Market prices of on-the-run securities are converted to yields, and a curve-fitting method (Treasury uses bootstrapping of forward rates plus monotone convex interpolation) produces a continuous curve from which constant-maturity yields are read.
concept.failure_modes: Curve shapes mix expected future rates, term premia, and supply/demand effects, so the curve alone cannot identify which driver dominates. Fitted curves are also model-dependent: different fitting methods produce slightly different yields at the same maturities.
concept.misconceptions: A common mistake is treating the yield curve as a forecast of future rates; Treasury itself states that the curve indicates what rates were and are, not what they will be.
concept.example: On a day when the 2-year Treasury yields 4.0% and the 10-year yields 4.3%, the 2s10s segment of the curve is upward sloping by 30 basis points.
